\chapter{Good Night}
\label{ch:ar-good-night}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone good night in Arabic and explain why the phrase actually talks about the morning.}

Say tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr, translate it as 'may you wake into goodness', and trace tuṣbiḥ back to ṣabāḥ al-khayr's own root.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr]{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير} (tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr) — wishing the morning, not the night}

\label{lesson:AR-C27-tusbih-ala-khayr}



\begin{quote}
Every \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} you've learned in other languages wishes a peaceful \textbf{night}. Arabic's everyday version does something completely different — it skips the night and wishes the \textbf{morning} instead.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير} — \textquotedblleft{}may you wake into goodness\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} (\textbf{tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr}) is the most common everyday Arabic \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} — but it literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{may you wake up into goodness}.\textquotedblright{} Break it down:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{تصبح}} (\emph{tuṣbiḥ}) — the ordinary imperfect (\textquotedblleft{}you become\textquotedblright{}) of \textbf{\ar{أصبح}} (\emph{aṣbaḥa}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to become morning, to wake up}\textquotedblright{}) — the \textbf{exact same root}, \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}} (ṣ-b-ḥ), as \textbf{ṣabāḥ} in \textbf{ṣabāḥ al-khayr} (\textquotedblleft{}good morning,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 1). No special subjunctive or jussive form is involved — a plain statement doing the work of a blessing, the same way English \textquotedblleft{}you'll sleep well\textquotedblright{} can function as a wish without any special grammar.
  \item \textbf{\ar{على}} (\emph{ʿalā}) — \textquotedblleft{}upon.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{\ar{خير}} (\emph{khayr}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{goodness}\textquotedblright{} — the same word already met in \textbf{masāʾ al-khayr} (\textquotedblleft{}good evening\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

Put together: not \textquotedblleft{}sleep well,\textquotedblright{} but \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{may your waking be good}.\textquotedblright{} (This particular form, \emph{tuṣbiḥ}, addresses one \textbf{man}; a woman is \emph{tuṣbiḥī} {[}\ar{تصبحي}{]}, a group is \emph{tuṣbiḥū} {[}\ar{تصبحوا}{]}.)

\begin{culture}
Here's the genuinely different part: the everyday \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} of English, French, German, and Spanish wishes something about the \textbf{night itself}. Arabic's everyday version does the opposite: it's grammatically about the \textbf{morning that follows}, built from the same \textquotedblleft{}waking\textquotedblright{} root already hiding in \emph{ṣabāḥ}. Notice what's genuinely absent: \textbf{\ar{ليل}} (\emph{layl}, \textquotedblleft{}night,\textquotedblright{} last lesson) doesn't appear anywhere in this phrase at all. It reuses pieces you already have (\emph{ṣ-b-ḥ}, \emph{khayr}) but points them at a \textbf{different moment in time} than every other language's farewell.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}may you wake into goodness\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shared root — tuṣbiḥ and ṣabāḥ, both from ṣ-b-ḥ
  \item the honest twist — this \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} is really about the morning, not the night
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{May you wake up into goodness}.\textquotedblright{}) What root does \emph{tuṣbiḥ} share with \emph{ṣabāḥ al-khayr}? (\emph{\textbf{Ṣ-b-ḥ}}, \textquotedblleft{}morning/to become morning.\textquotedblright{}) Unlike English, French, and German's \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} what moment in time does Arabic's everyday version actually point to? (\textbf{The morning that follows}, not the night itself.)
\end{tcolorbox}
